corrections.how: Holder: `research` (stateless, memory off, no accounts). On this install four settings are needed, not one. (1) `browser.enabled: true`: the family's config has it off today and the tool answers 'Browser control is disabled' until it is on. (2) `agents.entries.research.tools.alsoAllow: ["browser"]`. (3) If research runs sandboxed (the family default is sandbox mode `all`): add `browser` to `agents.entries.research.tools.sandbox.tools.allow` as well, because sandbox tool policy is a second gate and its built-in deny list includes `browser`. (4) Also if sandboxed: `agents.entries.research.sandbox.browser.allowHostControl: true` to reach the host-managed profile, with the WEB-03 hook requiring `target: "host"`; or build the sandbox browser image instead. Running research with `sandbox.mode: "off"` (what the 9 Oct review of F019 recommended, since it holds no exec or file tools) removes (3) and (4): the host browser is then the default target. Profile: a dedicated managed profile (for example `browser.profiles.research` with its own `cdpPort` and `headless: true`). `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`. The WEB-03 hook allows research only `status`, `tabs`, `open`, `navigate`, `snapshot`, `text`, `screenshot`, `close` and blocks every other action. Placement comparison: (1) host-managed profile: own user data directory, works headless, least bot-detection trouble, but runs on the host so container network rules do not cover it; (2) sandbox browser container: strongest isolation, but the image is not in the npm package, it cannot run with network `none`, and the docs say it trips bot detection more often; (3) the `user` and `chrome` profiles attach to a real signed-in Chrome and are wrong for research (WEB-05).

corrections.how: Plugin with `api.on("before_tool_call", handler, { matcher: ["browser"] })`; the docs also offer a stricter tier, `api.registerTrustedToolPolicy`, which runs before ordinary hooks. It reads `ctx.agentId`, `ctx.requester` and `event.params`. A call can hide its target in three places and the hook must read all of them: the URL is taken from `targetUrl` first and `url` second; an act can arrive as a top-level `kind` or inside a nested `request` object; and act kind `batch` carries a nested `actions` array. Rules per agent, all failing closed: reject any `profile`, `target` or `node` other than the one assigned, and treat a missing `profile` as a block or fill in the assigned one, because an omitted profile means the default profile; reject `systemProfile`, `into`, `domains` and `dashboard`; allow `open`/`navigate` only when every URL field present is on an exact hostname list; allow only a listed subset of the tool's 24 actions; treat act kinds as an allowlist as well: block `batch`, `evaluate`, `press`, `clickCoords`, `drag`, `wait`, `resize` and `type` with `submit`, block any call whose top-level and nested kinds differ, and return `requireApproval` with `allowedDecisions: ["allow-once", "deny"]` for `fill`, `type`, `select`, `click` and the `upload` action. Block gated actions outright when `ctx.requester` is absent (scheduled and system runs). Unknown agent, missing field, unknown kind or parse error returns a block; the runner itself blocks the call if the handler throws or runs past 15 seconds. Prompts are answered in the same chat that raised them with a typed `/approve <id> <decision>`; the family's config already has `approvals.plugin` enabled in `session` mode. Lobster is not the gate here: it is disabled in sandboxed contexts.
caveats: The hook sees tool parameters, not page meaning: a click carries a snapshot ref, not the button's label, so code cannot tell 'Next' from 'Submit'. The safe rule is an approval on every click inside a form, which becomes tedious after three prompts.
Approval waits are capped at ten minutes and an unanswered request denies.

Do not rely on scheduled runs having no approval route: the docs say an automation's approval card is delivered to whatever approval surface is connected and the run waits. Keep unattended runs away from gated actions in the hook itself, by blocking when no requester is attached to the call.

On iMessage the approver list is the channel allowlist, not the requester: the roadmap already notes that approvals are not tied to the person whose agent asked, so prompts must go only to the asking chat.
A navigation allowlist in a hook checks the URL the agent asked for, not where redirects or page scripts go next.
With `open` and `navigate` allowed, a link straight to a file is saved into the managed downloads directory without the `download` action ever being called.
The parameter names come from the installed 2026.9.7 tool schema and can change on upgrade; the hook needs a contract test that runs after every OpenClaw update.

corrections.how:
Holder: `

-portal`, one per adult, because accounts are per person and shared agents hold none. Memory off, session-scoped sandbox, tools `browser` only: no web_search, no web_fetch, and as a sub-agent it cannot have `message`. It needs the same four switches as WEB-02 (`browser.enabled`, `alsoAllow`, the sandbox tool allow list, host control). Profile: `browser.profiles.portal-

` (managed, own user data directory and `cdpPort`, not headless while a person logs in), with the browser's password manager and sync turned off. Login: the parent signs in by hand in that profile; the operator opens it with `openclaw browser --browser-profile portal-

open ` and the parent uses Screen Sharing to the Mac mini. The agent is never given a password; the docs permit owner-supplied credential fills, so this is a family rule backed by the hook's block on typing. WEB-03 hook: profile pinned, hostnames limited to that one portal, actions limited to `open`, `navigate`, `snapshot`, `text`, `close`.

-main reaches it through `sessions_spawn` with `subagents.allowAgents` and `completionTarget: "parent"`, so the answer comes back as text in a private turn of

-main instead of going straight to chat; the agent is told to answer in a fixed short form (titles, dates, numbers). `llm-task` is not the gate here: it is a separate optional tool this agent does not hold, and it checks only its own single completion. Excluded by rule: lunch-payment portals, banks, health portals, any page with a pay button.
corrections.safety:
All three trifecta legs meet in one agent: account data, page content, and navigation as a way out. It is defensible only with the way-out leg cut hard: one hostname, read-only actions, no message tool, no memory. The fixed-format reply is a convention, not an enforced limit: what the sub-agent says reaches

-main as free text, and

-main holds memory and a search tool. The hostname rule is a hook and the docs say the browser's request interception is not a firewall, so a residual leak path remains until the browser sits behind an egress proxy. No payments, no settings changes, no CAPTCHA solving. Recommendation: defer until WEB-03 has been tested against the injection suite.

corrections.how: Mechanism choice: an email already sent by the service. One-time parent step in the lunch portal: enable the low-balance email for each student and set the amount. Then get those messages into the school mailbox (F051): best by putting that mailbox on the account as the alert address if the portal allows it, otherwise by a forwarding rule from the parent's mail, tested once. Reader: the tool-less, memory-less `school-mail` agent with the sender on its allowlist; the line is rendered by the F056 digest job. No web_fetch, no browser, no API. Topping up stays with the parent.
caveats: You hear about it only when the balance crosses the threshold. "What is the balance right now" needs a login and belongs to the parent's app.

The service's app can already notify the phone; the gain is one digest instead of another app to check.

The bundled IMAP watcher admits a message only if its From address is on the allowlist and, by default, the message passes an aligned DMARC check done locally. A forwarded alert keeps the lunch service's From address, so it gets through only when the service's signature survives the forward; a rejected message never reaches the reader and nothing is texted.

corrections.description: Due-date, overdue and hold-ready notices for every family library card folded into the daily digest, using the emails the library already sends. Whether anything arrives before the due date depends on the library: the example library's own emails are due-date and overdue notices, and the early reminders its patrons relied on came from a third-party service that is closing. A full "what is checked out" list on demand is the one library question that needs a login, and it is the natural first (and maybe only) use of WEB-04.
corrections.how: Mechanism choice: service email. Set every card's notification preference to email (parents' and kids' cards) and get those notices into the household or school mailbox (F051), preferably by using that mailbox as the notification address. The tool-less reader extracts title, due date and pickup-by date for the digest (F056) and offers a reminder (F007) when the notice arrives before the due date. Library events: subscribe the library's calendar feed if it has one (G012). Full list on demand: WEB-04 with the library as the single allowlisted host. Plain web_fetch is not an option because account pages need a login. Renewing and placing holds stay with the parent.
caveats: Notices cover single items at or after their due date, earlier only if the family's library sends a courtesy reminder; they never show the whole shelf, which needs the login path. A day-before reminder is possible only when the email arrives early enough.
The example library notes that a third-party reminder service that worked from patron accounts is being discontinued: tools built on library accounts from the outside are fragile.
Each card usually has one email address; a parent has to set the kids' cards up once.
The library's own app shows all of this already.

The bundled IMAP watcher accepts mail only from allowlisted senders that pass an aligned DMARC check; forwarded library notices may be dropped silently, so point the cards' notification address at the mailbox directly or test the forward once.

reason:
Mechanism and sources are sound and it is config-only once the research agent exists. The safety claim is too strong: llm-task validates one completion inside research, but what research hands back to

-main is ordinary sub-agent text that nothing schema-checks, and a string field can hold any text anyway. Also, the `summarize` fallback is not installed and has its own Firecrawl switch.

corrections.how:
Mechanism choice: plain `web_fetch`, which reduces a page to its main content; schema.org also defines a Recipe vocabulary (`recipeIngredient`, `recipeInstructions`, `recipeYield`) that recipe sites can embed.

-main hands the URL to research with `sessions_spawn` and `completionTarget: "parent"`; research fetches, makes one `llm-task` call with a small schema (title, yield, ingredients[], steps[], source URL, fetched-at) and returns that JSON as its result;

-main scales quantities and proposes list items (F032), written only after a yes. The schema shapes the answer but is not an enforced gate: the result reaches

-main as ordinary sub-agent text. Fallbacks in order: WEB-02 `text` action for script-rendered pages; a host-side `summarize --extract` wrapper for video recipes (the CLI is not installed; pin `--firecrawl off` in the wrapper).
corrections.safety:
The untrusted page is read by research only. What crosses to

-main is asked to be schema-shaped JSON, which keeps honest output tidy but does not bound a hostile one: the sub-agent's reply is free text with no schema step on

-main's side, and a string field can carry anything. The real limits are that research holds nothing private, list writes need the parent's yes, and

-main has no browser or fetch. Nothing private goes to research: a URL and a serving count.
caveats: The fetch returns the readable article text. It is not documented to return the page's embedded Recipe data, so the model parses ingredients from prose and can drop a line. Always include the source link.
Some recipe sites sit behind bot walls or paywalls and return nothing; say so instead of guessing.
The phone's reader view and recipe-keeper apps already do the clean-up; the added value is the hand-off to the shared grocery list.
Scaling quantities is arithmetic done by a language model: fine for a stew, worth a second look for baking.
On today's config no agent has `web_fetch` or `sessions_spawn` and the `llm-task` plugin is not enabled; all three are config changes that arrive with F019 and F082.
unverified: Whether web_fetch output ever includes a page's JSON-LD blocks: a search of the installed code found no JSON-LD handling in the fetch extractor, but no live recipe page was fetched.
How many of the recipe sites this family uses embed schema.org Recipe data.
Whether llm-task's isolated completion works through the family's per-person custom provider ids; its allowed-model list has to name them.

corrections.how: Mechanism: the managed browser's `pdf` action, run by research in the logged-out profile (WEB-02 with `pdf` added to its allowed actions). The export is written into the gateway's own media store on the host and the tool returns its path as `FILE:<path>`; it is not placed in the `/tmp/openclaw` download root. It is only useful as the front half of 'print it' (the F080 print plugin takes the path and must accept only paths inside that store) or of the document vault (F044). When the link is already a PDF, the print plugin downloads it itself; the `pdf` tool only analyses documents. Receipts: mechanism choice is the service's email, forwarded as it is.
corrections.safety: Logged-out public pages only. A logged-in "save my order receipt" would need WEB-04 on a shopping account and is not built. Browser outputs are untrusted input; they sit in the gateway's media store until the print plugin's own checks, and the path that reaches the plugin is model-relayed text, so the plugin validates it.
unverified: Whether the `message` tool can attach a file from the gateway's browser media folder in iMessage Basic mode without widening the attachment roots.
Whether a hook can leave `pdf` enabled while blocking `download` for the same agent; they are separate actions in the schema, so it should.
Whether PDF export also works on a profile that is not headless; the research profile here is headless.

corrections.how: A decision record plus three guards: leave `tools.web.fetch.provider` unset and do not install `@openclaw/firecrawl-plugin` (once selected, its fetch fallback works without a key); add no remote CDP profile for a hosted browser; and if the `summarize` CLI is ever wrapped for research (WEB-11), pin `--firecrawl off` in the wrapper, because that CLI has its own Firecrawl fallback.
